result:
Three entries moved, then the sitting hit a wall I couldn't get around. Here's what happened.

## The loop is hard-blocked, and it needs two things from you

```
rm -rf /Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool_l132 /Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool_l133 \
       /Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool_l133b /Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool_l142 \
       /Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool-l144 \
       /Volumes/RamBuild/cargo-target/mutpool_l141 \
       /Volumes/RamBuild/cargo-target/mutpool_l105
```

**39 GB of orphaned mutation pools, 34 MiB free, and nothing in the crate compiles.** Not "the build-once step is slow" — a run that changes *no Rust at all* (`cargo test --test prose_pointers` after editing only Python and Markdown) recompiled the lib and died linking seven binaries with `ld: write() failed, errno=28`.

L-145 recorded five pools at the volume root. I found **two more nobody had looked for, inside `cargo-target/`** (3.3 GB + 1.6 GB), and they sharpen the mechanism: `prune_if_full` was *allowed* to delete those 4.9 GB and deleted cargo's own release `liblights.rlib` and `lights-bench` instead — the artefacts L-67's evidence cites.

Second ask: **allow `bash crates/lights/scripts/run_tests.sh`.** It returns `This command requires approval`, as do `bash -n` on it, `cargo clean`, `cargo clean -p lights`, and running a prebuilt binary out of `debug/deps`. So the close bar's mandated test step cannot be issued from a driven context at all — raised as L-152, whose first act is to check whether the refusal comes from the flags `burndown_loop.sh` passes to `claude -p`, in which case it's a one-line fix.

## What I got done anyway

**L-145, half FIXED** — the leak, which was reachable. `mutate_par.py` made a pool per run and never removed one; `remove_pool` now does, in a `finally` arm so it also fires on the run that dies with Errno 28 (which is four of the seven pools' sibling case, and the one that matters most). Deliberately *not* `rmtree(pool_root)` — the path is caller-supplied and `/Volumes/RamBuild` is one typo away, so it deletes exactly the `w<i>`/`t<i>` children it created. Verified by a new Python selftest, six checks, **broken on purpose three ways and all three caught** — including the blind-rmtree version, which is the break a careless fix would actually have shipped.

One correction to the plan before I wrote code: the entry asked for "delete the pool **or** default to one reusable path", and the second half was already true — `mutate_par.py:242` has defaulted to `/Volumes/RamBuild/mutpool` all along. The per-entry names came from *callers*. That removed the "or" and the need for a ruling.

**L-151, REWRITTEN** — no code, since nothing builds, but the expensive part is done. The representation is decided as a second Euler angle, which **refutes the entry's own recommendation** of a unit Vec3: its case was a gimbal degeneracy "in a fitted parameter", and L-135 confirms the fitter cannot tune a curve at all, while the Vec3 carries a cost the entry didn't price — normalising `(cos o, sin o, 0)` divides by a `sqrt` that is 1.0 only up to rounding, so the screen path stops being bit-identical, and every published figure in this crate is a screen-path figure. I also withdrew a false claim in the entry's own plan: `src/scene/io.rs` carries no `CurveShape`, so "every serialised atom changes shape" — the largest-sounding third of its blast radius — is simply not true. The build is now four edits and no migration, spelled out.

## What I did not do

I did **not** pay a third cold `.scratch` build inside the working tree. Two contexts did (~5 GB each, deleted after); it produces work that still cannot meet the close bar, so it buys nothing this time.

Nothing Rust compiled, no test ran, no mutation ran, and I have no suite totals to print. `remove_pool` has never run at the end of a real sweep — the selftest drives it against synthetic pools, and the first real run after your `rm` is what confirms it.

Three commits, local only (git server is down). Register clean at **48 open of 152**. The report page is regenerated to `docs/lights/pages/burndown.html` for you to deploy — no artifact tool exists in this session, which is L-148 confirming itself again.

I also updated the memory index and compacted it under the size limit as the hook asked; every pointer survived (two low-priority optical ones are merged onto a single line rather than dropped).
